questions.q: Why does the query use COUNT(DISTINCT soh.SalesOrderID) instead of COUNT(*) for OrderCount?
options: COUNT(*) is not valid T-SQL syntax
Joining to SalesOrderDetail repeats each SalesOrderID once per line item, so COUNT(*) would count line items rather than orders
SalesOrderID can contain NULL values that COUNT(*) would skip
DISTINCT is required any time GROUP BY is used
questions.explain: Because the FROM starts at SalesOrderDetail, an order with three line items appears three times, so counting distinct order IDs is needed to get a true order count.

questions.explain: DATEPART(QUARTER, ...) gives the current quarter number, which the formula converts to that quarter's starting month, then DATEFROMPARTS assembles day 1 of that month.

questions.q: Why does the WHERE clause use >= on the start date and < on the end date rather than <=?
options: T-SQL does not support the <= operator on date columns
It makes the query run faster regardless of correctness
It creates a half-open range that avoids double-counting a boundary date between quarters
It is required whenever COUNT(DISTINCT ...) appears in the SELECT list
questions.explain: Using >= on the start and < on the end means a date exactly on the next quarter's first day is correctly excluded rather than counted in both ranges.

questions.q: Why can a correct run of this query never return more than four rows?
options: The query's TOP clause restricts it to four rows
Production.ProductCategory has exactly four rows in AdventureWorks2012 -- Bikes, Components, Clothing, and Accessories
SQL Server limits GROUP BY results to four rows by default
Only four sales territories exist in AdventureWorks2012
questions.explain: Since the result is grouped by category name and AdventureWorks2012 has exactly four product categories, the output can have at most one row per category -- four at most.

questions.q: What governs which columns must appear in this query's GROUP BY clause?
options: Aggregate functions like SUM must also be listed in GROUP BY
GROUP BY must list every column referenced anywhere in the query
Every column in SELECT that isn't wrapped in an aggregate function (here, pc.Name) must appear in GROUP BY
Only columns from the first table listed in FROM need to be grouped
questions.explain: This is the standard GROUP BY rule: non-aggregated SELECT columns must be part of the grouping, which is why pc.Name appears in GROUP BY.
